posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: I've never seen a true-color DCG hologram (just pseudocolor) but evidently they do exist. Judging by published material only, the Chinese group has done the most interesting work in recent years. They published in SPIE and elsewhere, and used Jeff's basic MBDCG system, but with the addition of rhodamine 6G. I've mentioned this group previously on the forum. But instead of spending a lot of time on this, I would just mix a little DCG, fire up my 315, and start making some holograms. The more complicated stuff can come later.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
I'd think that an achromatic DCG hologram of a piece of white porcelain would be "true color". How about an achromatic hologram of a black & white photograph? 

I've lit Kubota and Rallison's work for exhibition and would say it was as real looking as it can be. I remember seeing silver in the clothing of a doll figure that really looked like silver, with no color breakup at all. The black hair was a real looking black with witish highlights, not milkish haze. There was subtle pastle colors. I'll bet that if the real doll was next to that reconstruction, and most importantly lit with the determination as durring recording, that it would be a "true color" hologram as well.

Designating a hologram as "true color" suggests to me a very technical view of holography, which I share. Could we also say that any hologram that hasn't changed color since it was made is true color?

I think I remember Jeff saying that G307 and MB are incompatable but I can't find the post. The wiki lists a green sensitive dye that is compatible with MB. I am very interested in trying this but I really know nothing.

Yes I brought this matter up in my paper at the 2006 Symposium in Wales . ( [http://www.holographer.org/](http://www.holographer.org/)

Basically Colin the G307 system for green light needs acidic dichromate with as high a concentration as possible without getting crystallization whereas 

the "panchromatic" plan with MB needs alkaline "dichromate" which means actually Chromate salt in really low concentration because it is now not supposed to absorb any green or red light itself but to act as a rejuvenator of light bleached dye and in so doing it gets reduced to CrIII and thus crosslinks the gelatin. You cannot use the MB dye with acidic dichromate unfortunately so you need a green absorbing dye which is photobleachable just like MB under mildly alkaline conditions using chromate ------ the dye I found is Safranine 'O' . 

Erythrosin works too on its own but may be less compatible with MB .

Jeff

Yes this was a remarkable achievement . It used a 2 layer system to get the red sensitivity did'nt it?

Some years ago I visited a lab in Belgium run by Alex Cobljin. We managed to make an impressive 5 x 4" DCG denisyuk of 2 little porcelain gnomes

with bright blue and red coats. Alex had HeCd and HeNe lasers . We used my MBDCG (TMG) system to get this result which looked impressively

panchromatic even though it had no green contribution back then , it was just 442nm and 633nm. I mention this because if you had a blue laser 

source then the MBDCG system automatically gives you blue sensitivity because although the chromate level is low its absorption in 442nm is very strong. 

Currently I am working with my colleague Tristram Cox here to get a 405nm Blue Ray laser diode out of its housing kit. This is the much more powerful writer laser rather than just the reader type. The unit cost was about £280 -----ie less than a tenth of what it would have been as a stand -alone laser diode unit! We have to be careful to get it running in a "permanently " on mode without damage. It should be in a TEM00 mode, and great for photoresist experiments but probably too far into the violet to be good for panchromatic DCG. Costs of these UV lasers are bound to come right down over the next years I suppose but I cannot wait till then. I will report on any future success here later. 

Jeff

posts.author: Danny Bee
posts.content_md:
here is a Panchromatic DCG formula

i recived this from Hans

Here are the details given in the paper: 

1. Soak 2g of French inert gelatin in 40ml deionized water at 25C for 12 hours. 

2. Heat the suspension in a thermostatic water bath to about 45C, then keep the temperature and stir the mixed solution slowly for 15 minutes. 

3. Add 2.5ml of 0.5% potassium chromate solution while stirring at 45C for 2 minutes. 

4. Add 0.6ml of 25% TMG solution while stirring at 45C for 2 minutes. 

5. Adjust the pH value to 9.18 with TMG or acetic acid solution at 45C. 

6. Add 0.3ml of 0.4% MB solution to the suspension while stirring at 45C for 5 minutes, then add 0.3ml of 0.2% R6G solution to the suspension while stirring at 45C for 5 minutes. 

7. Pipette out 8ml of the mixed solution and spread it over 8X24cm2 leveled optical glass, keep it in dark and dry in horizontal position at 25C for 24 hours. 

Processing: 

a) Soak in F5 solution at 25C for 1 minute 

b) Wash holographic plate in running water at 25C for 30 seconds 

c) Swell holographic plate in warm water at 31C for 1.5 minutes 

d) Dehydrate in 60% isopropyl alcohol bath at 25C for 1 minute 

e) Dehydrate in 90% isopropyl alcohol bath at 25C for 1 minute 

f) Dehydrate in 100% isopropyl alcohol bath at 25C for 2 minutes 

g) Dry hologram rapidly with flowing hot air 

My note: I assume the "F5 solution" is Kodak F-5 Hardening Fixer, which according to one of my books, contains sodium thiosulfate 240g, sodium sulfite 15g, acetic acid 28% 48ml, boric acid 7.5g, potassium alum, dodecahydrate 15g, water to make 1 liter.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
You are right about the F5 formula. It works nice wonders on MBDCG in that it clears the MB out of the plate very quickly and gives the gelatin a hardening bias. The hardening bias allows higher swelling bath temperatures, decreases milkiness, and reduces chances of patches of different colour in the hologram.

The disadvantage is that a 100ml bath is exhausted after only two plates. I found that giving the plate a uniform exposure of one seventh the normal exposure time, followed by a longer water wash (to remove all traces of MB and TMG) gives similar results.

I don't know if the F-5 would be required for panchromatic DCG, where Rhodamine 6G is used for the green sensitivity.
